added_claim_errors: "confirm the office will charge before the 15th": expenses count when the service is provided, not when the office charges, so this is misleading
"spending $1,500 on stuff you wouldn't otherwise buy to save $680 is a loss": the numbers don't match any real scenario (at the $680 cap the spend-down is $1,220), so this is confused
"$1,220+ evaporates on January 1": loosely worded. Forfeiture is measured at the end of the run-out, and 2026 claims filed during it still count
Run-out is "usually ~90 days after Dec 31": typical but plan-specific, and not sourced
The answer gives a Rev. Proc. 2025-32 link for the $680 cap, which is right. It gives no Pub 969 or Notice 2005-42 citation for the grace period or the use-it-or-lose-it rule.

"the carryover only happens if you're still employed and still enrolled in the FSA in the new plan year": the enrollment condition is stated as certain, but it varies by plan and the key could not verify it

The table labels ~$680 carried over as the "best case" and ~$1,220 forfeited as the "realistic math": misleading, because a grace-period plan covers all $1,900. The grace period only comes later as a "nuance".
The uniform-coverage question ("Is my full $1,900 available now?") is a tangent: the $1,900 is already the remaining balance. The rule matters for the 2027 election, which the answer never mentions.
"you usually have until March-April to submit receipts": a typical run-out range, unverified
A "not tax or benefits advice" disclaimer and an extra "two traps" section add length without content

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start and give the right $680 carryover cap and the ~$1,220 forfeited figure. Neither says all $1,900 is certainly lost, and both send the person to HR with the run-out question. Both suggest moving the dental work into December, and both list plausible eligible items. Neither mentions the 2027 open-enrollment election (point 8). A lays out the carryover, grace-period and neither branches explicitly. It gives the March 15, 2027 cutoff with a "book early in March" instruction, and it says "neither" means losing it all. It is also shorter. B frames carryover as the "realistic" case and leaves the grace period to a later "nuance". It hedges the grace branch ("might be reimbursable", "~March 15") and never states that all of it is forfeited if there is neither feature. It is longer, with a table, a disclaimer and a tangential uniform-coverage item, and it asserts a definite enrollment condition for carryover that varies by plan. B's one edge is stating that the service must happen by Dec 31, which comes closer to the incurred-date rule (point 6). A's "charge before the 15th" wording is a small blemish. Overall A is slightly better.
